newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW - Tenaga to plan for expansion.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Tenaga to plan for expansion.

text.p: The new chairman of Malaysia's power utility Tenaga Nasional Berhad laid out plans on Monday to upgrade and expand electricity delivery in the country, and said it aimed to boost efficiency against burgeoning demand.

"Our core business is to deliver electricity to consumers... If we are able to deliver that mission, that task, the rest will fall into place," Executive Chairman Ahmad Tajuddin Ali said at a news conference.
"The credibility with the consumers, the leverage position with the government and regulators will be improved," he said.

A 12- 15-hour power blackout on August 3 brought the entire peninsular Malaysia to a virtual standstill, angering consumers and embarrassing politicians, and led Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad to say he did not rule out breaking Tenaga's monopoly on electricity distribution.

Tenaga has earmarked four billion ringgit in 1996 (US$1.6 billion) and five billion ringgit (US$2 billion) in 1997 to upgrade and expand its electricity generation, transmission and distribution facilities, Tajuddin said.

"We have funds for this year, for next year, we may be going out to borrow in order to fund the projects," he said, but acknowledged that the company might face poor reception due to the fallout from the August blackout.

The company planned to raise about US$1 billion in 1997 in international capital markets and was open to various options on how to go about doing it, Tajuddin said. Tenaga has raised bonds of up to a 100-year maturity period in the past.
The chairman said he was not in favour of raising tariffs at present.

"At this point, I'm not in favour of a tariff increase...I don't think whatever I submit today would be credible for a tariff increase if it is not seen that we've tried to put our house in order first, enhance our productivity," he said.
The August outage brought the company unwelcome publicity and led the government to appoint Britain's National Grid Group Plc as a consultant to examine Tenaga's operations.
Tajuddin was appointed as chairman shortly after the power outage on September 1, replacing Ani Arope whose term expired at the end of August.
But Tajuddin said he did not think the consultancy study, which is due by the end of the month, would recommend Tenaga's monopoly be broken.
"I have had meetings with the senior consultants and from remarks they have made and other information...we don't believe that event would trigger the loss of monopoly," he said.
Tenaga has contingency plans should it lose its position, he added without elaborating.

Malaysia expects annual gross domestic product growth of over eight percent and 14 to 16 percent growth in the industrial sector. It needs to tackle a 14 to 16 percent growth in annual electricity demand, Tajuddin said.
